L88@P3: When I first took office as Surgeon General in 2014, I didn’t view
L89@P3: loneliness as a public health concern. But that was before I embarked
L90@P3: on a cross-country listening tour, where I heard stories from my fellow
L91@P3: Americans that surprised me.
L92@P3: People began to tell me they felt isolated, invisible, and insignificant.
L93@P3: Even when they couldn’t put their finger on the word “lonely,” time and
L94@P3: time again, people of all ages and socioeconomic backgrounds, from
L95@P3: every corner of the country, would tell me, “I have to shoulder all of life’s
L96@P3: burdens by myself,” or “if I disappear tomorrow, no one will even notice.”
L97@P3: It was a lightbulb moment for me: social disconnection was far more
L98@P3: common than I had realized.
L99@P3: In the scientific literature, I found confirmation of what I was hearing.
L100@P3: In recent years, about one-in-two adults in America reported experiencing
L101@P3: loneliness.1-3 And that was before the COVID-19 pandemic cut off so
L102@P3: many of us from friends, loved ones, and support systems, exacerbating
L103@P3: loneliness and isolation.
L104@P3: Loneliness is far more than just a bad feeling—it harms both individual
L105@P3: and societal health. It is associated with a greater risk of cardiovascular
L106@P3: disease, dementia, stroke, depression, anxiety, and premature death.
L107@P3: The mortality impact of being socially disconnected is similar to that
L108@P3: caused by smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day,4 and even greater than
L109@P3: that associated with obesity and physical inactivity. And the harmful
L110@P3: consequences of a society that lacks social connection can be felt in
L111@P3: our schools, workplaces, and civic organizations, where performance,
L112@P3: productivity, and engagement are diminished.
L113@P3: Given the profound consequences of loneliness and isolation, we have
L114@P3: an opportunity, and an obligation, to make the same investments in
L115@P3: addressing social connection that we have made in addressing tobacco
L116@P3: use, obesity, and the addiction crisis. This Surgeon General’s Advisory
L117@P3: shows us how to build more connected lives and a more connected society.
L118@P3: If we fail to do so, we will pay an ever-increasing price in the form of our
L119@P3: individual and collective health and well-being. And we will continue
L120@P3: to splinter and divide until we can no longer stand as a community or
L121@P3: a country. Instead of coming together to take on the great challenges
L122@P3: before us, we will further retreat to our corners—angry, sick, and alone.
L123@P3: Letter from the Surgeon General
L124@P3: Dr. Vivek H. Murthy
L125@P3: 19th and 21st Surgeon General
L126@P3-4: of the United StatesOur Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on the Healing Effects of Social Connection and Community 5
L127@P4: We are called to build a movement to mend the social fabric of our nation.
L128@P4: It will take all of us—individuals and families, schools and workplaces,
L129@P4: health care and public health systems, technology companies,
L130@P4: governments, faith organizations, and communities—working together to
L131@P4: destigmatize loneliness and change our cultural and policy response to it.
L132@P4: It will require reimagining the structures, policies, and programs that shape
L133@P4: a community to best support the development of healthy relationships.
L134@P4: Each of us can start now, in our own lives, by strengthening our
L135@P4: connections and relationships. Our individual relationships are an
L136@P4: untapped resource—a source of healing hiding in plain sight. They
L137@P4: can help us live healthier, more productive, and more fulfilled lives.
L138@P4: Answer that phone call from a friend. Make time to share a meal. Listen
L139@P4: without the distraction of your phone. Perform an act of service. Express
L140@P4: yourself authentically. The keys to human connection are simple, but
L141@P4: extraordinarily powerful.
L142@P4: Vivek H. Murthy, M.D., M.B.A.
L143@P4: 19th and 21st Surgeon General of the United States
L144@P4: Vice Admiral, United States Public Health Service
L145@P4: Each of us can start now, in our
L146@P4: own lives, by strengthening our
L147@P4: connections and relationships.
L148@P4: Loneliness and isolation represent profound threats to our health and
L149@P4: well-being. But we have the power to respond. By taking small steps
L150@P4: every day to strengthen our relationships, and by supporting community
L151@P4: efforts to rebuild social connection, we can rise to meet this moment
L152@P4: together. We can build lives and communities that are healthier and
L153@P4: happier. And we can ensure our country and the world are better poised
L154@P4: than ever to take on the challenges that lay ahead.
L155@P4-5: Our future depends on what we do today.Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation: The U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on the Healing Effects of Social Connection and Community 6
L156@P5: A Surgeon General’s Advisory is a public statement that calls the
L157@P5: American people’s attention to an urgent public health issue and provides
L158@P5: recommendations for how it should be addressed. Advisories are
L159@P5: reserved for significant public health challenges that require the nation’s
L160@P5: immediate awareness and action.
L161@P5: This advisory calls attention to the importance of social connection for
L162@P5: individual health as well as on community-wide metrics of health and
L163@P5: well-being, and conversely the significant consequences when social
L164@P5: connection is lacking. While social connection is often considered
L165@P5: an individual challenge, this advisory explores and explains the
L166@P5: cultural, community, and societal dynamics that drive connection and
L167@P5: disconnection. It also offers recommendations for increasing and
L168@P5: strengthening social connection through a whole-of-society approach.
L169@P5: The advisory presents a framework for a national strategy with specific
L170@P5: recommendations for the institutions that shape our day-to-day
L171@P5: lives: governments, health care systems and insurers, public health
L172@P5: departments, research institutions, philanthropy, schools, workplaces,
L173@P5: community-based organizations, technology companies, and the media.
L174@P5: This advisory draws upon decades of research from the scientific
L175@P5: disciplines of sociology, psychology, neuroscience, political science,
L176@P5: economics, and public health, among others. This document is not an
L177@P5: exhaustive review of the literature. Rather, the advisory was developed
L178@P5: through a substantial review of the available evidence, primarily found
L179@P5: via electronic searches of research articles published in English and
L180@P5: resources suggested by a wide range of subject matter experts, with
L181@P5: priority given to meta-analyses and systematic literature reviews. The
L182@P5: recommendations in the advisory draw upon the scientific literature and
L183@P5: previously published recommendations from the National Academies
L184@P5: of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine, the Centers for Disease Control
L185@P5: and Prevention, the American Heart Association, and the World
L186@P5: Health Organization.
L187@P5: The findings and recommendations in the advisory are also informed by
L188@P5: consultations with subject matter experts from academia, health care,
L189@P5: education, government, and other sectors of society, including more
L190@P5: than 50 identified experts who reviewed and provided individual detailed
L191@P5: feedback on an early draft that has informed this advisory.
L192@P5: For additional background and to read other Surgeon General’s
L193@P5: Advisories, visit SurgeonGeneral.gov

L320@P7: colleagues, and neighbors are just some of what create

L36: ## Summary
L37: The Congressional Budget Office regularly publishes reports presenting its baseline projections of what the federal budget and the economy would look like in the current year and over the next 10 years if laws governing taxes and spending generally remained unchanged. This report is the latest in that series, presented in an abbreviated version to facilitate work on other Congressional priorities.
L38: The budget projections are based on CBO’s economic forecast, which reflects developments in the economy as of December 4, 2024. They also incorporate legislation enacted through January 6, 2025.
L39: ### The Budget Outlook
L40: #### Deficits
L41: In CBO’s projections, the federal budget deficit in fiscal year 2025 is $1.9 trillion. Adjusted to exclude the effects of shifts in the timing of certain payments, the deficit grows to $2.7 trillion by 2035. It amounts to 6.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025 and drops to 5.2 percent by 2027 as revenues increase faster than outlays. In later years, outlays increase faster than revenues, on average.
L42: In 2035, the adjusted deficit equals 6.1 percent of GDP—significantly more than the 3.8 percent that deficits have averaged over the past 50 years.
L43: Interactive
L44: #### Debt
L45: 
L46: From 2025 to 2035, debt swells as increases in mandatory spending and interest costs outpace growth in revenues. Federal debt held by the public rises from 100 percent of GDP this year to 118 percent in 2035, surpassing its previous high of 106 percent of GDP in 1946.
L47: 
L48: Interactive
L49: #### Outlays and Revenues
L50: Federal outlays in 2025 total $7.0 trillion, or 23.3 percent of GDP. They remain close to that level through 2028 and then rise, reaching 24.4 percent of GDP in 2035 (if adjusted to exclude the effects of shifts in the timing of certain payments). The main reasons for that increase are growth in spending for Social Security and Medicare and rising net interest costs. Revenues total $5.2 trillion, or 17.1 percent of GDP, in 2025.
L51: They rise to 18.2 percent of GDP by 2027, in part because of the scheduled expiration of provisions of the 2017 tax act. Revenues decline as a share of GDP over the next two years, falling to 17.9 percent in 2029, but then generally increase, reaching 18.3 percent in 2035.
L52: Interactive
L53: #### Changes in CBO’s Budget Projections
L54: 
L55: The deficit for 2025 is $0.1 trillion (or 4 percent) less in CBO’s current projections than it was in the agency’s June 2024 projections, and the cumulative deficit over the 2025–2034 period is smaller by $1.0 trillion (or 4 percent). The largest contributor to the cumulative decrease was growth in projected collections of individual income taxes, driven by greater projections of taxable income in CBO’s economic forecast.
L56: 
L57: ### The Economic Outlook
L58: #### Economic Growth
L59: In CBO’s projections, economic growth cools from an estimated 2.3 percent in calendar year 2024 to 1.9 percent in 2025 and 1.8 percent in 2026 amid higher unemployment and lower inflation. The Federal Reserve continues reducing interest rates through the end of 2026, which supports economic growth. Real GDP then grows by 1.8 percent per year, on average, through 2035. Roughly four-fifths of the growth over that period is due to increases in the productivity of the labor force.
L60: The rest is due to increases in the size of the labor force.
L61: Interactive
L62: #### Inflation
L63: 
L64: The overall growth of prices slows slightly in 2025. Inflation as measured by the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE) falls from an estimated 2.5 percent in 2024 to a rate roughly in line with the Federal Reserve’s long-run goal of 2 percent in 2027 and stabilizes thereafter.
L65: 
L66: Interactive
L67: #### Interest Rates
L68: 
L69: The Federal Reserve began reducing the federal funds rate (the rate financial institutions charge each other for overnight loans) in September 2024. In CBO’s projections, those reductions continue through the end of 2026. Longer-term interest rates, such as the rate on 10-year Treasury notes, decline through the end of 2026 and then remain roughly flat.
L70: 
L71: Interactive
L72: #### Changes in CBO’s Economic Projections
L73: Since June 2024, when CBO published its previous full economic forecast, the agency’s projections of the average growth rate of real GDP over the 2024–2026 period have changed little. CBO raised its forecast of the average unemployment rate for 2024 to 2026 and lowered its forecast of employment growth over that period. Inflation is expected to be slightly higher, on average, in 2025 and 2026 than the agency projected in June. The forecast of long-term interest rates for 2026 is also higher.
L74: After 2026, CBO’s current and previous forecasts are generally similar.
L75: When October 1 (the first day of the fiscal year) falls on a weekend, certain payments that ordinarily would have been made on that day are instead made at the end of September and thus are shifted into the previous fiscal year. Because those shifts can distort budgetary trends, CBO often presents adjusted projections of deficits and outlays that treat the payments as if they were not subject to the shifts.
